p2.key: Second order in A: from experiment 1 to 2, [A] doubles ([B] constant) and the rate quadruples (0.50 → 2.00), i.e. 22.
First order in B: from experiment 2 to 3, [B] quadruples ([A] constant) and the rate quadruples (2.00 → 8.00).

Rate = k[A]2[B]

Note the orders come from experiment, not from the coefficients in the equation (B has coefficient 2 but is first order).

0.50 = k(0.200)2(0.200)
k = 0.50/0.008 = 62.5 dm6 mol−2 hr−1

Units: rate/(conc)3 = mol dm−3 hr−1 ÷ mol3 dm−9.
Step 1 is rate-determining, because it is the slowest step; the overall rate cannot be faster than the slowest step.

Step 1. It is the slower step, so it must have the higher activation energy (fewer collisions have enough energy to react).

Step 2 involves a highly reactive F radical, so it is fast with a low Ea.

Rate = k[NO2][F2]

The rate expression contains the species in the rate-determining step (step 1), each to the power of its coefficient there.

(i) Rate constant, k: the constant of proportionality linking the rate to the concentrations of reactants as they appear in the rate expression (rate = k[A]m[B]n). Activation energy, Ea: the minimum energy colliding particles must have for the collision to result in reaction.

(ii) Rate: mol dm−3 s−1; k (second order): mol−1 dm3 s−1.

(i) Maxwell–Boltzmann curves: y-axis “number (fraction) of molecules”, x-axis “energy”; both start at the origin and never touch the x-axis. T2 (higher) curve has a lower, broader peak shifted to higher energy; areas under the two curves are equal.

(ii) Mark Ea on the energy axis: at higher temperature a greater fraction of molecules have energy ≥ Ea (larger area beyond Ea), so more collisions are successful per unit time.

(iii) A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower Ea, so more molecules have enough energy to react.

(i) Plot ln k (−20 to 0) against T−1 (1.2–1.9 × 10−3 K−1) with labelled axes; the points lie on a straight line with negative gradient.

(ii) Gradient = Δ(ln k)/Δ(1/T) ≈ −7.3 / 3.4 × 10−4 ≈ −2.15 × 104 K (−2.0 to −2.4 × 104).
Since ln k = ln A − Ea/RT, gradient = −Ea/R
Ea = 8.314 × 2.15 × 104 = 1.79 × 105 J mol−1 = 179 kJ mol−1 (166–200 accepted).

(iii) Extrapolate the line to 1/T = 0: the intercept is ln A. Or substitute a value of ln k, 1/T, Ea and R into ln k = ln A − Ea/RT and solve for A.

(i) O3: first order — experiments 1→2: [NO] constant, [O3] doubles, rate doubles.
NO: first order — experiments 1→3: [NO] ×3 and [O3] ×3, rate ×9; tripling O3 accounts for ×3, so tripling NO gives the other ×3.
Rate = k[NO][O3]

(ii) Experiment 1: 0.660 × 10−4 = k × (1.00 × 10−6)(3.00 × 10−6)
k = 2.2 × 107 dm3 mol−1 s−1

(iii) Rate = 2.2 × 107 × 4.50 × 10−6 × 7.20 × 10−6 = 7.13 × 10−4 mol dm−3 s−1
(or rate3 × 3/2 × 8/10).

(i) For a first-order reaction t½ = ln2/k = 0.693/k
k = 0.693/1.62 × 104 s = 4.28 × 10−5 s−1 (units required).

(ii) ln k = ln A − Ea/RT → Ea = (ln A − ln k)RT
T = 834 + 273 = 1107 K
Ea = [3.219 − (−10.059)] × 8.314 × 1107 = 1.22 × 105 J mol−1 = 122 kJ mol−1
(Using 834 instead of kelvin gives 92.1 kJ — a common error.)

(iii) Bimolecular slow step involves two N2O molecules:
Slow: N2O + N2O → N2 + N2O2 (or → N4O2)
Fast: N2O2 → N2 + O2 (or N4O2 → 2N2 + O2)

Energy profile with y-axis enthalpy (potential energy), x-axis reaction progress: products (P) below reactants (R) because ΔH = −82 kJ mol−1 (exothermic), ΔH arrow pointing down. Two humps: the uncatalysed path with the higher Ea and the catalysed path with a lower Ea(cat), both labelled and measured from the reactant level.

Either method:

  • Gas volume: Mg and acid in a conical flask connected by an airtight bung/delivery tube to a gas syringe (or inverted measuring cylinder over water).
  • Mass loss: flask on a top-pan balance, not sealed (cotton wool plug) so H2 escapes.

Then: record volume of H2 (or mass) at regular time intervals with a stopwatch; plot volume (or mass loss) against time and find the gradient (tangent) to get the rate, or use rate ≈ 1/time.

The slope (gradient) decreases with time and eventually becomes zero (rate decreases).

Because the acid is used up, its concentration falls, giving fewer collisions per second (the curve levels off when the acid is consumed, as Mg is in excess).

(i) Curve B: less steep than A at the start and levels off at half the final volume of A (acid is limiting and half as many moles of H2SO4). Lower concentration → acid particles more widely spaced → fewer collisions per unit time.

(ii) Curve C: steeper than A but levels off at the same final volume (same amount of acid). Powder has a larger surface area → more frequent collisions between acid particles and Mg.
First order with respect to H2SO4: the graph of rate against concentration is a straight line through the origin, so rate is directly proportional to [H2SO4].

Rate = k[H2SO4] (zero order in Mg).

k = gradient = rate/[H2SO4], e.g. 0.008/0.9 ≈ 8.9 × 10⁻³ (accept ±2 × 10⁻³).

Units: (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹)/(mol dm⁻³) = s⁻¹.

At a higher temperature k would be larger (more particles have E ≥ Ea).

The reaction has a high activation energy, so at room temperature almost no collisions have enough energy to react (methanol is kinetically stable even though the reaction is thermodynamically spontaneous).

Ignition supplies energy so molecules have E ≥ Ea; the highly exothermic reaction then releases enough heat to keep itself going.
The overall order is the sum of the orders (powers) of the concentration terms in the rate expression, e.g. for rate = k[A]m[B]n, overall order = m + n.

A: zero order – Exps 1→2: [A] doubles, [B] constant, rate unchanged (3.0 × 10⁻⁴).

B: second order – Exps 1→3: [B] doubles, [A] constant, rate increases ×4 (3.0 × 10⁻⁴ → 1.2 × 10⁻³), and 2² = 4.

Orders stated without justification score only 1.
Rate = k[B]² (A does not appear because it is zero order).

k = rate/[B]² = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ / (2.0 × 10⁻³)² = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ / 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ = 75

Units: (mol dm⁻³ min⁻¹)/(mol dm⁻³)² = mol⁻¹ dm³ min⁻¹ (minutes essential, as the rates are per minute).
Doubling the pressure doubles the concentration of each gas. Rate = k[B]², so rate increases by 2² = 4 times (A being zero order has no effect).

Heterogeneous: the catalyst is in a different phase/state from the reactants (here a solid with gases).

How it works (any two): reactants are adsorbed onto active sites on the surface; bonds in the reactants are weakened; molecules are held in a favourable orientation; this provides an alternative pathway with lower Ea.

(i) Rate increases: the catalyst provides an alternative route with a lower activation energy, so more collisions have E ≥ Ea.

(ii) Rate decreases: molecules have lower average kinetic energy, so fewer collisions have E ≥ Ea (and collisions are less frequent).

(i) Exothermic profile: reactants (N2 + 3H2) higher than products (2NH3); ΔH (−92 kJ) shown as the drop from reactants to products; Ea shown from reactants up to the transition state (activated complex). Label axes.

(ii) The catalyst lowers Ea by providing an alternative reaction pathway, so more collisions are successful.

(iii) Heterogeneous: catalyst in a different phase from the reactants (solid Fe, gaseous reactants). Reactants are adsorbed onto active sites on the surface, where bonds are weakened and they react.

p2.key:
(i) Exp 1→2: [NO] constant, [O2] doubles, rate doubles → first order in O2. Exp 2→3: [NO] doubles and [O2] doubles, rate ×8; ×2 from O2, so ×4 from NO → second order in NO. Rate = k[NO]2[O2].

(ii) The slow (rate-determining) step involves only one NO and one O2, giving rate = k[NO][O2], not two NO.

(iii) One step with 2NO + O2 fits the rate equation, but a termolecular step needs three particles to collide simultaneously with correct orientation — very unlikely.

(iv) Fast pre-equilibrium makes [NO3] ∝ [NO][O2]; slow step rate ∝ [NO3][NO], so overall rate ∝ [NO]2[O2].

(v) e.g. 2NO ⇌ N2O2 (fast), then N2O2 + O2 → 2NO2 (slow). [N2O2] ∝ [NO]2, so rate ∝ [NO]2[O2].

NO: second order — compare experiments 1 and 3: [H2] constant, [NO] doubles, rate increases ×4 (2.53 → 10.10 × 10−6), and 4 = 22.

H2: first order — experiments 1 and 2: [NO] constant, [H2] doubles, rate doubles.
Rate = k[NO]2[H2] (orders from (a); the stoichiometric coefficients are not used).

Using experiment 1: 2.53 × 10−6 = k(0.100)2(0.100)

k = 2.53 × 10−6 ÷ 1.00 × 10−3 = 2.53 × 10−3 mol−2 dm6 s−1

Units: (mol dm−3 s−1) ÷ (mol dm−3)3 — third order overall.

Yes, it agrees.

The slow (rate-determining) step involves X and NO, so rate = k[X][NO]. X is formed in a fast equilibrium from H2 and NO, so [X] ∝ [H2][NO]. Substituting: rate = k′[H2][NO]2 — NO appears twice and H2 once up to and including the slow step, matching the rate expression. The three steps also add up to the overall equation.
A single step would need four molecules (2NO + 2H2) to collide simultaneously [1], with the correct orientation and enough energy — statistically extremely unlikely [1].
First order [1]: the graph is a straight line through the origin, so rate is directly proportional to [O2] [1].
Rate (y-axis) against [NO] (x-axis) [1]: an upward-curving parabola through the origin (rate ∝ [NO]2) [1].
Overall order = 2 + 1 = 3 (third order).
Doubling [NO] multiplies the rate by 22 = 4 (second order) [1]; halving [O2] halves the rate (first order) [1]. Overall: 4 × ½ = rate doubles [1].

Rate = k[NO]2[O2]

k = rate ÷ ([NO]2[O2]) = 6.3 × 10−4 ÷ [(3.0 × 10−2)2 × 1.0 × 10−2] = 6.3 × 10−4 ÷ 9.0 × 10−6

k = 70 mol−2 dm6 s−1

(i) Axes: [NO2] vs time [1]; curve starts at the origin, rises steeply then levels off [1]; draw a tangent at t = 0 — its gradient is the initial rate [1].

(ii) NO: second order — expts 1→2, only [NO] doubles, rate ×4.
CO: zero order — expts 2→3, only [CO] doubles, rate unchanged.
O2: zero order — expts 2→4, [NO] and [O2] both double and rate ×4, which is fully explained by NO alone.
The stoichiometric equation shows only the overall reaction, not the mechanism; order depends on the species in the rate-determining step, so it must be found experimentally.

(i) Half-life: time taken for the concentration of a reactant to fall to half its initial value [1]. For a first-order reaction t½ = ln2/k, which does not depend on concentration, so it is constant [1].

(ii) t½ = 0.693/k = 0.693/440 s−1 = 1.58 × 10−3 s

rate = k[N2O5]

First order: the concentration is raised to the power 1.

(i) rate = k[N2O5] – one N2O5 molecule takes part in the slow step.

(ii) Step 2 involves N2O5 and NO3, so rate ∝ [N2O5][NO3]. But NO3 comes from N2O5 in step 1, so rate = k[N2O5]2 (second order).

Why: species in or before the rate-determining step appear in the rate equation; intermediates are replaced by the reactants that form them.
The time taken for the concentration (amount) of N2O5 to fall to half its initial value.
It is constant – independent of the starting concentration of reactant.
The time taken for the concentration of a reactant (A) to fall to half its initial value.

From t = 0: [A] falls from 0.10 to 0.05 mol dm−3 in ≈1000 s.

From t = 2000 s: [A] ≈ 0.025 falls to ≈ 0.0125 at ≈3000 s, so half-life ≈1000 s (accept 900–1100 s).

First order, because the half-life is constant (independent of [A]).

rate = k[A]

k = rate / ([D]2[E]) = 3.75 × 10−5 / (1.35 × 10−2)3 = 3.75 × 10−5 / 2.46 × 10−6

k = 15.2 mol−2 dm6 min−1 (15.2–15.3)

Units: (mol dm−3 min−1)/(mol dm−3)3 for a third-order overall reaction.

At higher temperature, particles move faster, so collisions are more frequent (per unit time), and – more importantly – a greater proportion of collisions have energy ≥ Ea.

"More collisions" without reference to time is not accepted.

(i) 2ICl + H2 → I2 + 2HCl

(ii) ICl: first order. In Expts 1→2, [ICl] doubles at constant [H2] and the rate doubles.
H2: second order. In Expts 2→3, [H2] halves at constant [ICl] and the rate falls to ¼.

(iii) rate = k[ICl][H2]2

(iv) k = 5.00 × 10−3 ÷ (0.100 × 0.05002) = 20 mol−2 dm6 s−1.

(v) Doubling both concentrations multiplies the rate by 2 × 22 = 8: rate = 20 × 0.200 × 0.1002 = 4.00 × 10−2 mol dm−3 s−1.

(i) Step 1: P + Q → PQ (slow, rate-determining). Step 2: PQ + Q → R (fast). The RDS contains one P and one Q, which matches the rate expression.

(ii) Molecularity of the RDS = 2 (bimolecular).
4 minutes. 0.08 → 0.04 is one half-life, and for a first-order reaction the half-life is constant, so 0.04 → 0.02 also takes 4 min.

(i) A (the frequency/pre-exponential factor) reflects the frequency of collisions with the correct orientation (the geometric requirements of the reaction).

(ii) Ea is the minimum energy colliding particles need in order to react.

(iii) Any five of:

  • measure k at several different temperatures;
  • plot ln k against 1/T (T in K);
  • the graph is a straight line, ln k = −Ea/RT + ln A;
  • gradient = −Ea/R, so Ea = −R × gradient;
  • y-intercept = ln A, so A = eintercept.

(i) A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants. A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase.

(ii) One mark each:

  • reactants (CH2=CH2 + Cl2) drawn higher than the product (CH2ClCH2Cl), because ΔH is negative;
  • ΔH labelled as the gap between reactants and product;
  • Ea labelled from the reactants up to the peak;
  • a lower peak labelled Ecat.

NO: second order. Expts 1→3: [NO] doubles at constant [Br2] and the rate rises ×4 (3.20 → 13.0 × 10−3).
Br2: first order. Expts 2→1: [Br2] doubles at constant [NO] and the rate doubles. A reason is needed for each mark.
rate = k[NO]2[Br2]

3.20 × 10−3 = k × (2.00 × 10−2)2 × 5.00 × 10−3
k = 3.20 × 10−3 ÷ (2.00 × 10−6) = 1.60 × 103 dm6 mol−2 s−1. The reaction is third order overall, so the units are mol−2 dm6 s−1.

(i) No effect. k changes only with temperature.

(ii) The rate decreases. Doubling the volume halves both concentrations, so rate × (½)2 × ½ = ⅛ of the original. The official markscheme says “decrease (by a factor of 2)”, but the rate law predicts a factor of 8.
p2.flag: MS factor of 2 looks wrong: rate law predicts 1/8

p2.key: The reacting gases are adsorbed onto the catalyst surface, which provides a surface for the reaction. This gives an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful.

Draw an energy profile with enthalpy on the y-axis and reaction progress (time/course of reaction) on the x-axis. The reactants (2NO + Br2) are higher than the product (2NOBr), because the reaction is exothermic. Marks are for:

  • a curve clearly showing Ea without a catalyst;
  • a lower curve clearly showing Ea(cat) with a catalyst;
  • a labelled x-axis.
A correctly drawn endothermic diagram scores a maximum of [2].

(i) The reaction is zero order in Br2 and second order overall:
rate = k[CH3COCH3][H+]; rate = k[CH3COCH3]2; rate = k[H+]2.

(ii) For example, with rate = k[CH3COCH3][H+]: doubling [propanone] doubles the rate, doubling [H+] doubles the rate, and doubling [Br2] has no effect. Your predictions must match the expression you chose.

(iii) The half-life is constant: 1.6 → 0.8 mol dm−3 takes 10 s, 0.8 → 0.4 takes 10 s, and 0.4 → 0.2 takes 10 s. A constant t½ shows first order. Give at least two half-lives.

(iv) Observation: the orange-brown colour of bromine fades (follow it with a colorimeter). The acid is a catalyst: it speeds up the reaction by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, and it is not used up.

(i) Experiments 1→2: [NO] is constant and [O2] doubles; the rate doubles, so the reaction is first order in O2. Experiments 2→3: both concentrations double and the rate rises ×8 (2 from O2 × 4 from NO), so it is second order in NO.

(ii) rate = k[NO]2[O2]

(iii) k = 3.75 × 10−3 / [(3.50 × 10−2)2(1.75 × 10−2)] = 1.75 × 102 dm6 mol−2 s−1

(iv) Doubling the volume halves both concentrations. The rate is (½)3 = ⅛ of 7.50 × 10−3 = 9.38 × 10−4 mol dm−3 s−1.

(v) For example: NO + NO ⇌ N2O2 (fast), then N2O2 + O2 → 2NO2 (slow). The slow second step is rate-determining, and it involves 2 NO + 1 O2. Another accepted mechanism is NO + O2 ⇌ NO3 (fast), then NO3 + NO → 2NO2 (slow).

• At higher T, molecules have greater average kinetic energy, so they move faster.
  • Collisions are more frequent.
  • More importantly, a greater proportion of molecules have E ≥ Ea, so more collisions are successful.
  • Maxwell–Boltzmann sketch (number of particles vs kinetic energy): the 323 K curve is flatter and broader, with its peak shifted to the right. It has more area beyond Ea, and the area under both curves is the same.
Between experiments 1 and 2, [NO] is constant and [H2] doubles (2.0 → 4.0 × 10−3). The rate also doubles (4.0 → 8.0 × 10−3), so rate ∝ [H2]1: the reaction is first order in H2.

Second order in NO.

From experiments 1 and 4, [H2] is constant and [NO] is halved (4.0 → 2.0 × 10−3). The rate falls to ¼ (4.0 → 1.0 × 10−3), and (½)2 = ¼.
rate = k[H2][NO]2

Experiment 3: [H2] is 3 × the value in experiment 1, with the same [NO], so the rate is 3 × 4.0 × 10−3 = 1.2 × 10−2 mol dm−3 s−1.

Experiment 5: [NO] is ¼ of the value in experiment 1, with the same [H2], so the rate is (¼)2 × 4.0 × 10−3 = 2.5 × 10−4 mol dm−3 s−1.

k = rate / ([H2][NO]2) = 4.0 × 10−3 / [(2.0 × 10−3)(4.0 × 10−3)2] = 1.3 × 105 (1.25 × 105)

Units: mol dm−3 s−1 ÷ (mol dm−3)3 = dm6 mol−2 s−1

The rate-determining step must involve 2 NO and 1 H2, and the steps must add up to the overall equation. For example:

  • NO + NO ⇌ N2O2 (fast)
  • N2O2 + H2 → N2O + H2O (slow, rate-determining)
  • N2O + H2 → N2 + H2O (fast)

Three correct steps in sequence earn [2]; two earn [1].

• A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase (state) from the reactants, e.g. a solid catalyst with gaseous reactants.
  • Diagram (enthalpy vs reaction progress): reactants sit higher than products (exothermic), with a hump (transition state) above both.
  • A second, lower hump for the catalysed path sits above the reactants but below the uncatalysed peak. ΔH is unchanged.

(i) Zero order in A: in experiments 2→3, [A] doubles and the rate is unchanged. Second order in B: in experiments 1→2, [B] halves and the rate falls to ¼ (8.8 → 2.2 × 10−4).

(ii) rate = k[B]2 (= k[A]0[B]2)

(iii) k = 8.8 × 10−4 / (7.8 × 10−2)2 = 0.14 mol−1 dm3 min−1

Note that the time unit here is minutes, not seconds.

(i) rate = k[NO]2[Cl2]

(ii) Rate decreases by a factor of 4 (second order: (½)2 = ¼). The rate constant is unchanged – k depends only on temperature.

(iii) Axes labelled concentration / mol dm−3 and time / s. [NO] starts at 1.0 and falls with decreasing gradient; [NOCl] starts at 0 and rises (equal and opposite change, since 2 NO → 2 NOCl). Both curves level off at the same time – mark this as the equilibrium point.

The rate expression comes from the slow (rate-determining) step.

Above 775 K: rate = k[NO2][CO]

Below 775 K: rate = k[NO2]2 (CO enters only after the slow step, so it is zero order).

• When the reaction is zero order (rate = k).
  • When all reactant concentrations are 1.0 mol dm−3 (then rate = k × 1n).

ln k = −Ea/R × (1/T) + ln A, so gradient = −Ea/R.

Gradient = (9.2 − 8.4) / ((3.53 − 3.65) × 10−3) = −6.67 × 103 K

Ea = 6.67 × 103 × 8.31 = 5.54 × 104 J mol−1 = 55.4 kJ mol−1 (55.0–56.0 accepted; 55 454 J scores only [1] since kJ were asked for).
To keep the total volume constant (100 cm3), so the concentration of each species depends only on the volume of its own stock solution added – a fair comparison between experiments.

(i) Exp 1 → 3: [CH3COCH3] halved, rate halved → first order. Exp 1 → 4: [H+] halved, rate halved → first order. Exp 1 → 2: [I2] ×1.5, rate unchanged → zero order.
rate = k[CH3COCH3][H+]

(ii) Neither was fully correct: both were right about propanone, Hannah was right about H+, but both were wrong about iodine (zero order).

Total volume = 100 cm3, so each 10.0 cm3 of 1.00 mol dm−3 stock is diluted tenfold: [CH3COCH3] = [H+] = 0.100 mol dm−3.

k = rate / ([CH3COCH3][H+]) = 4.96 × 10−6 / (0.100 × 0.100) = 4.96 × 10−4 mol−1 dm3 s−1 (units must be correct; overall second order).

(i) Axes: x = kinetic energy (or speed), y = number/fraction of particles. A single Maxwell–Boltzmann curve starting at the origin, rising to a peak and tailing off towards (never rising from) the energy axis. Mark two activation energies, Ea(catalyst) lower than Ea(no catalyst); a larger area under the curve lies beyond the catalysed Ea. (Drawing two curves loses the third mark – the catalyst does not change the distribution.)

(ii) A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions have enough energy to react.

(i) Experiments 1→2: [OH−] doubles and the rate is unchanged, so the reaction is zero order in OH−. Experiments 1→3: both concentrations double and the rate doubles, so it is first order in X. Rate = k[X].

(ii) k = rate ÷ [X] = 4.0 × 10−3 ÷ 2.0 × 10−2 = 0.20 min−1.

(iii) 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH3)3CBr. It is tertiary, so it reacts by SN1 (rate depends only on [X]).

(iv) Slow step: C4H9Br → C4H9+ + Br−. Fast step: C4H9+ + OH− → C4H9OH.
k increases as T increases. As 1/T falls, ln k rises. Stating the Arrhenius equation alone does not earn the mark.

The Arrhenius plot has gradient = −Ea/R. From the line: gradient ≈ (−2 − (−5)) ÷ ((1.00 − 1.10) × 10−3) ≈ −30 000 K (accept −28 800 to −31 300).

Ea = 30 000 × 8.31 = 2.49 × 105 J mol−1 = 249 kJ mol−1 (accept 240–260).

After 10% has reacted, [N2O] = 0.9 × 0.200 = 0.180 mol dm−3.

Rate = k[N2O]2 = 0.244 × 0.1802 = 7.91 × 10−3 mol dm−3 s−1.

Using 0.200 instead gives 9.76 × 10−3, which scores 1 mark only.

The catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so the forward and reverse reactions speed up equally. Equilibrium is reached faster, but the position of equilibrium does not change.

(i) [NO(g)] means the concentration of NO in mol dm−3 at time t (not an equilibrium concentration).

(ii) Overall order = 3, so k = rate ÷ conc3 = mol dm−3 s−1 ÷ (mol dm−3)3 = dm6 mol−2 s−1.

(i) Rate = 34.1 dm3 ÷ 0.0400 s = 853 dm3 s−1 (or 1.50 mol ÷ 0.0400 s = 37.5 mol s−1). Units are required.

(ii) At higher temperature a much larger fraction of particles have energy ≥ Ea, so more collisions are successful (more frequent collisions also accepted).
The minimum energy that colliding particles need for a reaction to occur (the energy difference between reactants and transition state).
Yes, NO acts as a catalyst: it is used in step 2 but regenerated in step 3, so it is not consumed overall and does not appear in the overall equation.

(i) A reaction in which the system absorbs heat from the surroundings; ΔH is positive. ("Absorbs heat" alone is not enough.)

(ii) Sketch: one Maxwell–Boltzmann curve starting at the origin, rising to a peak, skewed tail approaching (not touching) the x-axis. Mark Ea(catalysed) to the left of Ea(uncatalysed) on the energy axis. Axes: y = number/fraction (probability) of particles with that energy; x = kinetic energy. Do not draw a second curve – the catalyst does not change the distribution, it lowers Ea.

(i) Dative covalent (coordinate) bond – the lone pair on N is donated to the electron-deficient B. Another example: CO, H3O+, NH4+, Al2Cl6, or a transition-metal complex.

(ii) Exp 1 → 2: [NH3] × 0.562, rate × 0.564 → first order in NH3; the other experiments show first order in BF3.
Rate = k[BF3][NH3]; overall second order.
Exp 4: k = 1.02 × 10−1/(3.00 × 10−1 × 1.00 × 10−1) = 3.40 dm3 mol−1 s−1 (units required).

(i) Intermediate: N2O2 (made in step 1, used in step 2).

(ii) H2 appears in the rate expression, so step 2 must be the slow, rate-determining step (step 1 is fast); the rate expression then includes both molecules of NO (via N2O2) and H2.

Since k2 ≫ k1, step 1 is the slow, rate-determining step. Step 1 involves two NO2 molecules, so rate = k1[NO2]2; CO only appears in the fast step and so is not in the rate expression – consistent with experiment.

From ln k = −Ea/RT + ln A, the gradient of ln k vs 1/T = −Ea/R.
Gradient from two points far apart on the line ≈ −2.2 × 104 K (accept −2.14 to −2.27 × 104 K; remember the x-axis is in 10−3 K−1).
